newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia calls on PNG rebels to release hostages.
newsitem.headline: Australia calls on PNG rebels to release hostages.

text.p: Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer on Saturday called on secessionist rebels on Bougainville island to release five Papua New Guinea soldiers held hostage since September 1996.
Downer welcomed the signing of a peace declaration by the Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA) and PNG-backed Bougainville officials in Christchurch on Friday.

"I think it would be a useful next step if the BRA were to release the five hostages that are being held on Bougainville. That would help to build a sense of confidence," Downer told Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio.
The soldiers were taken hostage after a rebel attack on the Kangu Beach government base in southern Bougainville, which left 11 soldiers dead.

Downer said the two-week peace talks in New Zealand had been a useful building block towards ending the nine-year revolt on the resource-rich island, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of the capital Port Moresby.

Officials from the BRA and its political wing and the Bougainville Transitional Government (BTG) signed a declaration pledging to negotiate with the government, which was not a party to the talks, starting in September.
They also agreed to work towards a ceasefire, the demilitarisation of Bougainville and for an international peacekeeping force.

"I think it has helped to create a sense of understanding between the different parties on Bougainville and the next stage will be the swearing in of a government in Papua New Guinea and then we look forward to the whole issue being taken from there," Downer said.
The Papua New Guinea parliament will sit on Tuesday to elect a new government after the recent election decimated the government of the former prime minister Sir Julius Chan.

Chan and several of his ministers lost their seats in a voter backlash to his government after it hired mercenaries to end the Bougainville revolt. The Chan government adopted a "hawkish" approach towards Bougainville after the failure of a series of earlier peace talks.

Papua New Guinea's first prime minister Sir Michael Somare is expected to form the next coalition government. Somare, who visited the five soldiers being held hostage late last year, is highly regarded as father of the nation and is expected to adopt a much more conciliatory approach towards Bougainville.
Thousands have died in the Bougainville conflict since landowners revolted in 1988 over damage caused by the huge Panguna copper mine, and the royalties they received from it.
The mine, now closed and used as the BRA's fortified headquarters, is owned by a unit of the Anglo-Australian giant Rio Tinto Ltd.
